Height (stature) or length indicates attained size or growth of adults and children. Long periods of inadequate food intake or
increased morbidity result in a slowing of skeletal growth and individuals being short for their age, or stunted. Consecutive

Weight
Weight is measured with digital weighing scales, using a pan, basket, sling, standing platform, or chair, depending on the age and
mobility of the people being measured. Weighing scales must be set on a hard, level, and even surface. Scales should be accurate,
sensitive, and robust. They must be carefully maintained, calibrated, regularly checked for accuracy using known weights, and
always set at zero before use. Weight is usually measured to the nearest 0.1 kg for adults and 0.01 kg for infants.
Weight measures total body mass but does not provide information on the proportions of fat, water, protein, and minerals.
Adults can be heavy for height if very muscular, over-fat, and big framed. With accurate scales, small changes in weight are detectable
but may not necessarily reﬂect change in body fat or lean body mass. In healthy persons, day-to-day variation in body weight is
